pos: n. (two men of the return: one who had taken a strange wife, and a priest of the house of Harim)
etymology: Hebrew Adna, pleasure, or delight, from adan, to be delicate or luxuriant; borne by two men, Ezra 10:30 and Nehemiah 12:15.
biblical_def: Adna is named twice in the books of the return, and the two settings could hardly be further apart in moral weight. The first Adna appears on a list of men who had to put away foreign wives: “And of the sons of Pahathmoab; Adna, and Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezaleel, and Binnui, and Manasseh” (Ezra 10:30). The charge laid on that whole company was explicit: “Now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives” (Ezra 10:11). The second Adna is a priestly head in the next generation: “Of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai” (Nehemiah 12:15), one of the chief of the fathers reckoned in the days of Joiakim — “And in the days of Joiakim were priests, the chief of the fathers: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah” (Nehemiah 12:12). The name means pleasure, and Ezra's charge uses the same root for God's pleasure. One man named delight is called to surrender his own in order to do God's; another of the same name serves at the altar. The register holds both without comment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Adna, pleasure, or delight; the name of one of the sons of Pahath-moab who had taken a strange wife, and of a priestly head of the house of Harim.

corruption_summary: Ezra's separation is read today as ethnic cleansing; Scripture presents it as covenant discipline over religion, with the men named and the obedience voluntary.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern treatment of Ezra 9 and 10 names it ethnic exclusion and reads the list of men as a casualty roll of a xenophobic purge. That reading cannot survive the text. The issue is never blood but worship: the strange wives brought the gods of the people of the land into households newly returned from a seventy-year judgment for exactly that sin. Scripture is full of foreign women brought into Israel by faith — Rahab, Ruth, the mixed multitude at Sinai — and honours them. What Ezra required was confession and separation from idolatry, and the men came forward and gave their names to it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that. The principle to recover is in the charge itself: make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure. Adna means pleasure, and the demand on him was to prefer God's pleasure to his own at the cost of his household. That is repentance with a price on it, which is the only kind the Scripture recognises.

pos: n. (a priest who went up with Zerubbabel, head of a father's house)
etymology: Hebrew Amoq, deep, from amaq, to be deep or unsearchable; named twice, Nehemiah 12:7 and 12:20.
biblical_def: Amok is named twice, and both times as a priestly head in the generation of the return. He closes the first list: “Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, Jedaiah. These were the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua” (Nehemiah 12:7). The second notice records who succeeded him: “Of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber” (Nehemiah 12:20). The company he belonged to is named at the head of the chapter: “Now these are the priests and the Levites that went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra” (Nehemiah 12:1), and the chapter dates the whole register: “These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest, the scribe” (Nehemiah 12:26). The name means deep. Nothing deep is recorded of the man; he went up from Babylon with the first company, took charge of a priestly house, and handed it to Eber. The depth of the restoration lay in men like him being willing to be ordinary in the right place.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Amok, deep; a priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and head of a father's house whose successor was Eber.

corruption_summary: The return from Babylon is remembered for its two or three famous names; Scripture names the priestly houses one by one, and a restoration is built out of such men.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular retellings of the return keep Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah and discard the rest, which leaves the impression that God restores a people through a handful of leaders. Nehemiah 12 was written against that impression. It names twenty-two priestly houses, gives the head of each in two successive generations, and dates the whole list. Amok is one line of it. The chapter insists that the restoration had a roster, and that continuity of office — this man, then Eber — was the mechanism by which worship resumed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of succession. A priestly house is not a career but a charge handed on, and the register's shape — of Amok, Eber — is the shape of faithfulness across a generation. The church that keeps no roster of who held what charge, and who received it next, has lost something Nehemiah thought worth writing down twice.

pos: n. (a man who stood beside Ezra at the reading of the law, and a sealer of the covenant)
etymology: Hebrew Anayah, the LORD hath answered, from anah, to answer, and the divine name; named twice, Nehemiah 8:4 and 10:22.
biblical_def: Anaiah is one of thirteen men who stood with Ezra on the day the law was read publicly in Jerusalem: “And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand” (Nehemiah 8:4). What happened next is the hinge of the whole restoration: “And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people; (for he was above all the people;) and when he opened it, all the people stood up” (Nehemiah 8:5), and then “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Two chapters later Anaiah is named again, among those who set their seal to the covenant: “Pelatiah, Hanan, Anaiah” (Nehemiah 10:22). His name means the LORD hath answered, and he is on record in exactly two places: standing where Scripture was opened, and signing his name to obey it. A dictionary could ask for no cleaner picture of what a man is for.

corruption_summary: Public reading of Scripture is treated as a ceremonial preliminary; in Nehemiah 8 it is the event itself, with the sense given and the hearers made to understand.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the regulative principle has been abandoned, the reading of Scripture in corporate worship shrinks to a few verses introducing something else, and the word distinctly in Nehemiah 8:8 has no counterpart in the service at all. The chapter describes the opposite order: a platform built for the purpose, thirteen men standing with the reader, the book opened, the people on their feet from morning until midday, and the sense given so that the hearers understood. The reading was the service.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that exposition is owed to the people and not optional — gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Anaiah's two appearances belong together. A man who stands where the book is opened will shortly find himself signing his name to its terms, because understanding Scripture has never left anyone where it found him.

pos: n. (one of the chief of the people who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Anan, a cloud, from the root meaning to cover or to bring a cloud; named once, Nehemiah 10:26.
biblical_def: Anan is named once, in the roll of those who put their seal to the covenant: “And Ahijah, Hanan, Anan” (Nehemiah 10:26). His name means a cloud — the same word used of the pillar that went before Israel and of the cloud that filled the house of the LORD. The covenant he sealed is described with unusual precision. It was entered by a company carefully defined: “And the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding” (Nehemiah 10:28). And its terms were severe: “They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes” (Nehemiah 10:29). Anan is a name on that document, and nothing else is told of him. It is enough: he bound himself, with his household, under oath, to the law of God.

webster_full: Hebrew Anan, a cloud.

And they stood up in their place, and read in the book of the law of the LORD their God one fourth part of the day; and another fourth part they confessed, and worshipped the LORD their God.
corruption_summary: Covenanting is reduced to a statement of values; the document Anan sealed carried an oath and a curse, and bound children as well as fathers.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religion has a vocabulary of commitment without consequence, and a covenant is heard as an aspirational statement that lapses quietly when inconvenient. Nehemiah 10 will not be read that way. Those who signed entered into a curse, and into an oath, invoking judgment upon themselves if they broke what they swore. They did so having first spent a fourth part of the day in the reading of the law, so no one could claim not to know the terms.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is household covenanting with knowledge. The text is careful that the sealers included their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding — not a formality imposed on the ignorant, but a family brought to the law and then bound by it. A man named for a cloud put his name to that, and the cloud in Scripture is where God shows Himself and where He hides.

pos: n. (a man of the children of Judah who dwelt at Jerusalem after the return)
etymology: Hebrew Athayah, the LORD is helper, or whom the LORD hath made opportune; named once, Nehemiah 11:4.
biblical_def: Athaiah heads the list of Judahites who settled the rebuilt capital: “And at Jerusalem dwelt certain of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin. Of the children of Judah; Athaiah the son of Uzziah, the son of Zechariah, the son of Amariah, the son of Shephatiah, the son of Mahalaleel, of the children of Perez” (Nehemiah 11:4). Five generations are given, which is a great deal of attention for a man who does nothing else in Scripture, and the reason is the strange difficulty the chapter opens with: “And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities” (Nehemiah 11:1). The city was walled but thinly peopled and dangerous to live in, so residence had to be assigned by lot. The next verse records the people's response to those who went willingly: “And the people blessed all the men, that willingly offered themselves to dwell at Jerusalem” (Nehemiah 11:2). Athaiah, of the line of Perez, is first among the men who took that risk, and his ancestry is given because the city needed to know whose houses had come back to it.

corruption_summary: Choosing where to live is treated as a private preference; in Nehemiah 11 it was a dangerous assignment taken by lot, and the willing were publicly blessed for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Mobility is now assumed to be a neutral good and a matter of personal fit, so a chapter in which men are brought by lot to live in a particular city reads as coercion. Nehemiah 11 is describing something the modern reader has little category for: a holy city rebuilt and still so exposed that ordinary families had to be drafted to inhabit it. Those who volunteered were blessed by the whole people, which tells you what the assignment cost.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that where a believer lives can be a work of obedience rather than of preference. Athaiah's genealogy is given to five generations because the restored city kept account of whose houses had returned to it. The church today needs men who will live where the work is, and a people willing to bless them for it.

pos: n. (a Levite who cried with a loud voice unto the LORD at the great confession)
etymology: Hebrew Kenani, planted, or established, a shortened form of the name built on kun, to establish; named once, Nehemiah 9:4.
biblical_def: Chenani is one of eight Levites named at the great day of confession: “Then stood up upon the stairs, of the Levites, Jeshua, and Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and cried with a loud voice unto the LORD their God” (Nehemiah 9:4). The day's pattern is given in the verse before: “And they stood up in their place, and read in the book of the law of the LORD their God one fourth part of the day; and another fourth part they confessed, and worshipped the LORD their God” (Nehemiah 9:3). Six hours of Scripture, then six hours of confession and worship, and Chenani is among the men who led the second half out loud. The call these Levites raised is recorded: “Then the Levites, Jeshua, and Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever: and blessed be thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise” (Nehemiah 9:5). The name Chenani means established, and what follows in that chapter is the longest recital of the LORD's dealings with Israel in the Old Testament, prayed by men who had just come home.

corruption_summary: Corporate confession has largely vanished from worship; Nehemiah 9 gives a fourth part of the day to it, led aloud by named men.
corruption_paragraphs: A service built around the preferences of the hearer has no room for six hours of reading followed by six hours of confession, and the loss is not merely one of stamina. Confession in Nehemiah 9 is historical and specific: the Levites recite what God did from Abraham to the exile and what Israel did in return, and the congregation stands under it. Where that is replaced by a general sense of inadequacy, the people never learn the shape of their own sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the day: the law read first, distinctly, and confession after it. Men cannot confess what they have not been told, which is why the reading came first and why the Levites gave the sense. Chenani's one recorded act was to cry aloud to God after hearing His law, which is the only sane response to it.

pos: n. (a son of Elioenai in the royal line of David after the exile)
etymology: Hebrew Delayah, the LORD hath delivered, or whom the LORD hath drawn out, from dalah, to draw water; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:24.
biblical_def: Dalaiah stands at the far end of the longest genealogy in Scripture that matters most: the royal line of David, carried on past the captivity. He is named in its last verse: “And the sons of Elioenai were, Hodaiah, and Eliashib, and Pelaiah, and Akkub, and Johanan, and Dalaiah, and Anani, seven” (1 Chronicles 3:24). A few verses earlier the line passes through the captivity itself — “And the sons of Jeconiah; Assir, Salathiel his son” (1 Chronicles 3:17) — and then through the governor of the return: “And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:19). Dalaiah is thus a descendant of David living generations after the throne was gone, in a province of Persia, with no crown in view. His name means the LORD hath delivered, and it is given to a man in a line that had just been carried to Babylon and brought back. The Chronicler ends his royal register there and leaves it open. The line did not stop; it ran on to Bethlehem.

corruption_summary: The Davidic line after the exile is treated as a dead dynasty kept on paper; Scripture keeps it because the promise to David had not failed.
corruption_paragraphs: A line of kings with no kingdom invites the judgment that the register is nostalgia, and the critical habit is to read 1 Chronicles 3 as a late construction propping up post-exilic claims. The Chronicler's own stated reason is different and plainer: “So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression” (1 Chronicles 9:1). The genealogies survived the judgment because God had made a promise attached to a family, and a promise attached to a family requires a list.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's covenant with David outlasted the loss of David's throne. Dalaiah held no office that Scripture names. He was simply in the line, and the line was the promise. When the fulness of time came, the Gospels opened with a genealogy, because that is how this promise was always going to be kept.

pos: n. (a Benjamite ancestor of Sallu, who dwelt at Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Hassenuah, the bristling, or the pointed, with the Hebrew article prefixed; named once, 1 Chronicles 9:7.
biblical_def: Hasenuah is named once, three generations back from a man who returned to the capital: “And of the sons of Benjamin; Sallu the son of Meshullam, the son of Hodaviah, the son of Hasenuah” (1 Chronicles 9:7). The form keeps the Hebrew definite article, which is why the name reads oddly in English; the same family name appears elsewhere without it. The register he anchors is the roll of those who resettled Jerusalem: “And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 9:3). The Chronicler has just told the reader why he keeps such lists at all: “So all Israel were reckoned by genealogies; and, behold, they were written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah, who were carried away to Babylon for their transgression” (1 Chronicles 9:1). Hasenuah himself lived before the deportation; his great-grandson lived after it. One name, spanning the judgment, is the Chronicler's way of showing that the house survived what the nation deserved.

And at Jerusalem dwelt certain of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin. Of the children of Judah; Athaiah the son of Uzziah, the son of Zechariah, the son of Amariah, the son of Shephatiah, the son of Mahalaleel, of the children of Perez;
corruption_summary: A name carried only as an ancestor looks like dead weight in the record; Chronicles uses such names to show which houses survived the deportation.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern reader meets a name like Hasenuah and sees an obstacle. The Chronicler saw a bridge. His whole ninth chapter is built to answer a question the returned exiles were actually asking — who belongs here, and by what right — and the answer is given by naming a resident, then his father, then his grandfather, then a man who lived before Babylon. The genealogy is a title deed, and the oldest name on it is the one doing the legal work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is stated in the chapter's own opening: Israel was carried away for their transgression, and yet Israel was still reckoned by genealogies. Judgment fell, and the record held. God is not careless with the houses He disciplines, and a name preserved across a deportation is a mercy written in a form we are too impatient to read.

pos: n. (the designation of Sanballat, chief adversary of Nehemiah)
etymology: Hebrew Horoni, a man of Horonaim, or of Beth-horon; used three times, always of Sanballat, Nehemiah 2:10, 2:19, 13:28.
biblical_def: Horonite is not a name but a label, and in Scripture it attaches to exactly one man. It appears the moment opposition to the rebuilding begins: “When Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, heard of it, it grieved them exceedingly that there was come a man to seek the welfare of the children of Israel” (Nehemiah 2:10). It appears again when the opposition turns to mockery and the charge of sedition: “But when Sanballat the Horonite, and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arabian, heard it, they laughed us to scorn, and despised us, and said, What is this thing that ye do? will ye rebel against the king?” (Nehemiah 2:19). The escalation is recorded plainly: “But it came to pass, that when Sanballat heard that we builded the wall, he was wroth, and took great indignation, and mocked the Jews” (Nehemiah 4:1). And it appears a last time when the danger has moved inside: “And one of the sons of Joiada, the son of Eliashib the high priest, was son in law to Sanballat the Horonite: therefore I chased him from me” (Nehemiah 13:28). The grandson of the high priest had married the adversary's daughter.

corruption_summary: Opposition to God's work is expected to come as persecution from outside; Sanballat's most dangerous move was a marriage into the high priest's own family.
corruption_paragraphs: Sanballat the Horonite is a study in how adversaries actually operate. He begins with grief and contempt, moves to public mockery, raises the political charge of rebellion against the king, attempts an ambush, and when none of it stops the wall he simply marries his daughter into the family of the high priest. The last tactic nearly worked, because it did not look like opposition at all. Nehemiah named it for what it was and expelled the man.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church's real danger is usually domestic. Nehemiah endured scorn, threats and conspiracy from without and survived them all; the breach came through an alliance of convenience at the top of the priesthood. Faithfulness requires watching the marriages and the appointments as carefully as the walls, and the willingness to say, as Nehemiah did, therefore I chased him from me.

pos: n. (grandfather of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe, and so of Huldah's husband)
etymology: Hebrew Charchas, very poor, or shining; named once in that form, 2 Kings 22:14, and as Hasrah in the parallel at 2 Chronicles 34:22.
biblical_def: Harhas is named once, and only to place a woman. When the book of the law was found in the temple and Josiah needed to know what it meant, the king's men went to a prophetess: “So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her” (2 Kings 22:14). The Chronicler gives the same line with the name in its other form, writing Hasrah where Kings writes Harhas, and the margin of the Authorized Version notes the two as one man. The discovery that set the errand in motion is reported twice: “I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 22:8), and “And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses” (2 Chronicles 34:14). The king's charge was urgent: “Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us” (2 Kings 22:13). Harhas's grandson kept the royal wardrobe; his grandson's wife told a king what the found book meant.

scriptures: So Hilkiah the priest, and Ahikam, and Achbor, and Shaphan, and Asahiah, went unto Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe; (now she dwelt in Jerusalem in the college;) and they communed with her.
And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.
And when they brought out the money that was brought into the house of the LORD, Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses.

Go ye, enquire of the LORD for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found: for great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book, to do according unto all that which is written concerning us.
corruption_summary: Huldah is enlisted today as a precedent for women in the teaching office; the text makes her a prophetess consulted privately by the king's messengers, not an elder in Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: Egalitarian argument reaches for Huldah as proof that the Old Testament authorised women to the teaching and ruling office, and Harhas's name survives in the middle of that dispute because the text identifies her by her husband's house. What 2 Kings 22 actually reports is that the LORD gave a word to a woman and that the king's delegation went to her house to receive it. Prophecy in Scripture is a gift sovereignly given and was given to Miriam, Deborah, Huldah and Philip's daughters; the priesthood and the eldership were never opened by it. Deborah judged Israel and summoned Barak to lead it; Huldah spoke the word of the LORD and did not serve at the altar.

The honest reading honours her without rewriting the offices. Josiah's men “communed with her” and carried back a true word of judgment and mercy, and the reformation that followed was the greatest in Judah's history. That is high honour, and it is the honour the text gives. Scripture's own order — male eldership in the church, with the gifts of the Spirit distributed as He wills to men and women alike — is not embarrassed by Huldah; it is illustrated by her.
